Ukraine’s military has run out of US Patriot missiles to repel ballistic attacks, which have one aim, the capital’s mayor says: to destroy morale By Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv. Photographs by Julia Kochetova Sat 22 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google V iktor, 23, Sofiia, 18, and their dog, Teddy, were bedding down for the night on Thursday at the Dorohozhychi metro station three stops from Kyiv’s city centre. The couple have sheltered here “every night for the past three weeks”, Viktor said, as the missile threat to the city worsened; the dog, only three months old, has been with them a fortnight. Teddy lies quietly, knowing no different a life. View image in fullscreen People sleeping at Dorogozhychi metro station for safety. The atmosphere in the Ukrainian capital has shifted in the past couple of months as the war has returned more sharply to the home front. Russian high-speed ballistic missiles are routinely targeting the city and Ukraine’s military have run out of the interceptors from the only weapon system that can stop them, US-made Patriots. The anxiety that hangs over the wartime city has intensified. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen (Clockwise from top left): Vitalii clears debris from around his damaged car with the help of a neighbour; the aftermath of a Russian night attack on Solomyanskiy district; a woman rests near the site of the attack. “Before, if you heard an air-raid warning you still had time to pack your stuff and get to the shelter. Now you have a warning and then in 30 seconds you have explosions, so you have no time,” Sofiia said. A night earlier, a wave of missiles targeted the city within minutes of the first warning, at 11.51pm. Sixteen people were reported killed after the missiles struck locations including residential blocks in the suburbs. Warnings of drone attacks followed for several more hours, fraying nerves after the opening hits. Russian ballistic missile attack sets Kyiv skyline ablaze City dwellers had been fearing a big attack on Wednesday night. It had been a few days since the last one – and there were also reports that Russian Tu-160 strategic bombers were flying to the war zone. They launch cruise missiles, but their presence in the air heralds a wider missile and drone attack. The lower hall at Dorohozhychi metro was packed by 10pm that night, Viktor said, with tents or people lying on ground sheets, almost no space left for the couple as they arrived. Earlier on Thursday, in the morning, the grim aftermath of the missile strikes on residential areaswas clearly visible. Two missiles struck the Solomianskyi district west of the centre, one shearing off the top floor of a 10-storey apartment block, killing two people, the second crashing into a disused building in the centre of a car park, reducing it to a scatter of rubble, while local people tried to see if there was any hope for their cars – the ones that were not completely burnt out. Kyiv book market burns after Russian missile strike The rear end of Vitalii’s car was smashed in by the blast, and it appears to be a write-off. The 42-year-old said he works for an insurance company, yet admitted he had not insured his own vehicle. After a while, however, the car started, remarkably, its engine having faced away from the blast. At first the impact of the overnight attack may be financial, but Vitalii said its real effect will be psychological. “We are alive, our arms and legs whole. We will go on. But now it will be more scary.” View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Vitalii, a Kyiv resident, checks his damaged car; a woman rests and checks her phone the day after the Russian attack. K yiv’s mayor, the former champion heavyweight Vitali Klitschko, arrived on the scene. “These attacks on the city have one aim – to drive people into depression,” he said. He is pressed about how many new bomb shelters the city has built, which might avoid people having to sleep in metro stations that reopen at 6am. He could offer no figure to one questioner. View image in fullscreen Vitali Klitschko, Kyiv’s city mayor, talks to the media at the site of a direct hit. Ukraine’s military no longer announces how many ballistics come in because it cannot stop them, though hits can easily heard from bedrooms right across the capital. In July, the last full month for which figures are available, 437 civilians were killed across Ukraine and 2,610 injured according to UN figures – the highest number recorded killed since May 2022. Ukraine civilian deaths chart Causes of civilian casualties in Ukraine Though it is August and the daily temperatures are frequently in the 30s, much of the talk is about the winter to come, when people expect to lose central heating and electricity as so many homes did last year when apartment temperatures in the worst-affected districts dropped to 4-5C. Kyiv’s infrastructure appears defenceless and those who can have long bought generators, batteries, electric radiators and anything else for emergency heating, but worries linger. View image in fullscreen A survivor of the night’s attacks holds a backpack containing her cat in Solomyanskiy district. “We are prepared to cope without electricity and without central heating – we did our homework, prepared the apartment and lasted last dreadful winter,” said Maria Hlazunova, who lives in the centre of the city. “But water … I’m afraid of lacking the opportunity to wash hands and food properly. Not to mention the toilet,” which she acknowledges is a particular source of anxiety. Residents know the city has only one wastewater treatment site, at Bortnychi. It has not yet been hit. Ukraine has defended itself by stepping up its attacks on Russia, long-range targeting first of the country’s oil refineries, leading to queues at petrol stations, and more recently by targeting warehouses, e-commerce sites that Kyiv says are also used by the military for logistics. It has been effective, though Russia has responded in kind – bombing and destroying warehouses just outside Kyiv, the medium-term economic consequences from the destruction uncertain. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The damaged Rozetka warehouse in Brovary, Kyiv region; a firefighter works at the warehouse after a Russian attack. Early on Thursday, a food distribution warehouse near Ukraine’s unused Boryspil commercial airport was completely destroyed by a missile attack. The fire spread because a succession of drone warnings – Shaheds were flying above – meant that emergency workers could not safely attend at first. When the Guardian visited in the afternoon, parts of the burnt-out site were still smouldering, and there were a handful of employees who recognised their jobs had disappeared in the wreckage. Viktoriia Ruban, the spokesperson for Ukraine’s state emergency services in Kyiv region, the area just outside the city, described a change in Russian military tactics. “Previously, the Russians would strike the Kyiv region at night. Now it’s three or four hours, then a strike; another three or four hours, then another strike. Whether it’s morning or daytime – it makes no difference now,” she said, and the observation applies also to the capital city where daytime alerts have become more common. 1:12 Barrage of Russian strikes devastates Kyiv – video Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, Ukraine’s most successful e-commerce distributor, showed a few journalists around the ruins of what was her company’s largest distribution hub near Brovary, north-east of Kyiv. It was a modern automated facility, built for $70m, capable of sending 100,000 parcels a day, and employing 1,000. But it was totally destroyed by three missiles on the night of August 4-5, the inferno so great that in places only bent-over cranes can be made out. View image in fullscreen Iryna Chechotkina, the co-founder of Rozetka, inside her company’s burnt-out distribution hub in Brovary, Kyiv region. It was a clearly difficult visit for the businesswoman, amid worries that more of the company’s warehouses could be struck, affecting Rozetka and the 50,000 vendors who rely on its service. But the wider military reality is fragile. “How can a country defend itself against ballistic threats if we have nothing with which to shoot them down?” she asked. “It’s very hard for me; I’m a mother of four and I’ve sacrificed time with them to build this place. It’s my life’s work.” Breaking into English, she added: “This is not easy.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Europe features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story More than 16 killed as Kyiv comes under intense Russian bombardment Volodymyr Zelenskyy sacks senior aide amid Ukraine corruption crisis Sacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponent Ukraine’s dismissed defence minister calls for wartime presidential election ‘Our task is to laugh at these enemies’: the Ukrainian unit posting drone videos of Russian soldiers’ last moments Moscow threat of ‘consequences’ will not alter UK support for Ukraine, says Burnham Finland halts deportation of Russian family who ‘risked everything’ to oppose Ukraine invasion Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Saul Loeb,andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty Images This Week in Trumpland Trump tariffs Analysis How to lose Trump’s trade war: test Canada’s resolve with threats to hockey sticks Adam Gabbatt The US president expected Ottawa to bow to tariff demands, but Canada is striking back – and it could cost Americans This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 14.49 EDT Share Earlier this year, a survey found that Canada , along with Switzerland , was the best-liked country in the world. We all know this kind of polling is about as scientific as a high school popularity contest, but at least anecdotally, Canadians have a reputation for being friendly and welcoming, respectful and polite. Many people would find it difficult to dislike Canadians. But not Donald Trump, who in a “hold my beer” moment this week demonstrated that he, at least, finds it easy to resent Canadians. The US president called the country “difficult and unreasonable”, and in a particularly hysterical moment, threatened to rename a lake , after trade talks collapsed. Days earlier, Trump had claimed a deal with Canada was imminent, which would avoid the new taxes. Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada Read more But, in a development that surely galled the Art of the Deal author, there was no agreement. Instead, Trump and his team demonstrated the art of collapsing the deal, as trade talks fell apart due to what Canada said were unreasonable, last-minute demands from the US side. It meant that the US tariffs duly came in on Saturday, applied to various Canadian exports including hockey sticks and tongue depressors, but if Trump expected Canada to bow to his demands – the president was seeking more favorable terms on things like steel and aluminum – he was disappointed. Instead, Mark Carney , the Canadian prime minister who has emerged as a rare world leader willing to stand up to Trump, said Canada had been “attacked”, and announced retaliatory tariffs on about $20bn worth of US goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment. All this means US consumers are seeing surging prices on all kinds of products – including toilet paper. My colleague Lauren Aratani reports that “the US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population”. And this outsize usage has grown more expensive. “Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials,” she writes. It’s fair to say that Canada’s retaliation upset Trump, who famously loves to win. On Tuesday, he claimed the US “is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer” – we’ll see how that goes – and has dubbed Canadian negotiators “clowns” . Earlier this week, Trump compared Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, unfavorably to his deceased brother Rob, the scandal-plagued former mayor of Toronto, whose time in office saw him admit to smoking crack cocaine and being “hammered” in public. And while Trump was flailing about, JD Vance was doing his best Scrappy Do, “lemme at ’em” impression, lobbing insults at Canada from the safety of a Republican rally in Maine. Vance claimed that Canada and China are “the two worst countries when it comes to trade policy anywhere in the world”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This Week in Trumpland A deep dive into the policies, controversies and oddities surrounding the Trump administration after newsletter promotion He added: “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry. Freudian slip. That was actually an accident.” The satisfied look on his face didn’t make it seem like one. Vance went on to add that Canada “quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. It was an interesting take, given the only country that has mused about invading Canada is the US – as recently as last year Trump was threatening to annex the nation . So in a nutshell: Donald Trump has led the US into an unsavory spat against the world’s most popular country, a scrap that could result in Americans – less than three months out from crucial midterm elections in which Republicans face an uphill battle – struggle to pay for a roll of toilet paper. Win! AD Russia-Ukraine War Kaliningrad: The Russian Exclave at the Center of a Nuclear Warning to NATO Russia has threatened to retaliate if NATO blockades or invades Kaliningrad, the latest incident of tensions being triggered over the strategic exclave. Add to My List Save A retired B-413 Soviet submarine docked next to the naval museum in Kaliningrad, Russia, on June 20, 2018. Ozan Kose/AFP via Getty Images A retired B-413 Soviet submarine docked next to the naval museum in Kaliningrad, Russia, on June 20, 2018. Ozan Kose/AFP via Getty Images Victoria Friedman 10/1/2026 | Updated: 10/1/2026 0:00 X 1 The Russian exclave of Kaliningrad has become the latest front for diplomatic tensions between Moscow and NATO allies. Russia has warned the Western defense alliance that it would be ready to resort to the use of nuclear weapons if NATO tried to attack or cut off the strategic region. What makes Kaliningrad, a small piece of land on the Baltic Sea between two NATO allies, a potential flashpoint for the Western defense alliance? Can the tensions be de-escalated? Here’s what you need to know, and how events unfolded. What Is Kaliningrad? Kaliningrad is a heavily militarized exclave—separated from the rest of Russia and sandwiched between NATO members Lithuania and Poland. Related Stories NATO Chief Calls for Calm Amid Russian Nuclear Threats Russia Threatens Nuclear Response to Any NATO Strike on Kaliningrad Sitting on the Baltic Sea, the territory is only around the size of the U.S. state of Connecticut and has a population of about 1 million people. It was formerly the German city of Königsberg and the capital of East Prussia. Kaliningrad then became part of the Soviet Union after the Red Army captured it in April 1945, as the Allies divided the former German territory after World War II under the Potsdam Agreement. Why Is It Important? Kaliningrad serves as the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is the country’s only year-round, ice-free port. Given its location, it provides Russia with the ability to project its military power into central and northern Europe. At the same time, being positioned between two NATO members makes it vulnerable, should the alliance decide to act against the territory. In the event of conflict, it would be difficult for Moscow to maintain supply lines. How Were Tensions Triggered? The nuclear threats from Moscow followed British media speculating on the Russian exclave as a Western target. Sky TV’s recent four-part documentary-drama series “The Wargame” depicts a fictional British Cabinet considering strikes on Russian territory, including Kaliningrad, after a simulated attack on the United Kingdom by Moscow. The iPaper said in a report on Sept. 26 that the territory “once seen as a threat to NATO could now be a weakness for Vladimir Putin that is waiting to be exposed.” The report also said a lot of Kaliningrad’s military personnel and firepower have been reassigned to Ukraine, leaving the exclave more vulnerable to attack. What Was Russia’s Initial Response? The Russian embassy in the UK, citing both the Sky docu-drama and the iPaper report, said on Sept. 29, “Any British or NATO military action against Russian territory would be met with a response using all means at Russia’s disposal, including nuclear weapons.” “Russia has repeatedly made clear that it neither seeks confrontation with NATO and Europe nor intends to attack them. But should anyone choose to unleash such a conflict, they must be under no illusion that Russia will respond accordingly,” it said. What Did NATO Say? This week, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte urged calm from allies and conveyed that Moscow should stop making threats about nuclear attacks. Speaking at Euronews’s Defence & Space Summit in Brussels, Belgium, on Sept. 30, Rutte said that there was no real risk that Russia would deploy nuclear weapons, dismissing the threat as hollow rhetoric aimed at distracting the West, trying to sow division among allies, and attempting to weaken support for Ukraine. “Of course, we had to reply and make clear to him that NATO is a defensive alliance,” Rutte said, adding that his message to Putin is to “stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it’s unhelpful. “And NATO is so much stronger than Russia, so there’s no way they can ever beat us.” He said that in terms of the risk of an attack, any buildup would be observed by allies, and countries on the eastern flank of NATO—such as the Baltic States or Finland—would sound the alarm. “There is no imminent threat to NATO territory,” Rutte said, saying that the threats come amid failures in Russia’s advances in its war with Ukraine. On the NATO side, he said, “we can allow a bit of calm.” However, he said that allies should continue to invest in defense and support Ukraine. Have Things Settled Down? It appears that Russia has toned down its rhetoric—and has also urged Europe to lower the temperature. On Oct. 1, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Russia has no plans to use nuclear weapons against Europe. “It is the Europeans who are thinking about Russia using nuclear weapons,” Peskov said, according to the Russian state-run news agency TASS. “We urge them to rein in their emotions and look at things objectively.” However, Peskov said that Russia would never allow the taking of Kaliningrad. “We need to tone down the rhetoric,” he said in comments to Izvestia. The Kremlin spokesman continued that Europe needs to understand that Kaliningrad is an integral part of Russia. “The Russian Federation will never allow anyone to challenge its status as an integral part of the country. At the same time, we believe that such rhetoric should not dominate. What is happening now is bad,” he said. Have There Been Tensions Before? Tensions have been rising over the territory and the Baltic region more broadly in the preceding months and years. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, NATO has sought to strengthen its eastern flank. Two new members have also joined: the previously neutral Nordic nations of Finland and Sweden. This means that Kaliningrad is surrounded on all fronts by NATO allies. These new members are not silent partners in the alliance, either. In August, Sweden announced its military would help surveil and protect Finnish territory until at least the end of this year, amid the deteriorating security situation. Russian embassies in Europe have also highlighted what Moscow says are hostile NATO military movements in ​the Baltic Sea. NATO has defended its increased presence in those waters as part of its response to concerns about threats to undersea communications cables and energy infrastructure. Russia has also criticized comments from some NATO member states about the exclave. In May, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys had told German newspaper ​Neue Zürcher Zeitung that NATO had to “show the Russians that ⁠we’re capable of penetrating the small fortress they’ve built in Kaliningrad.” Peskov said at the time that the comment “verges on insanity.” Owen Evans and Reuters contributed to this report. Moneycontrol World Desk October 11, 2026 / 16:18 IST Donald Tusk Poland has convened an emergency security meeting after authorities received information about a possible attack targeting Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, AFP reported, citing the interior ministry. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński and special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak ordered security action following information received by the police, ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka said on Sunday. Representatives of the Polish police, the Government Protection Service and the Internal Security Agency met at the agency’s counterterrorism centre on Sunday, Gałecka said, without disclosing further details about the suspected plot. The investigation comes amid heightened security concerns in Poland following a series of violent incidents at schools. A knife attack on Thursday killed a school caretaker. Separately, Western intelligence agencies have warned executives at European defence companies that Russia is intensifying efforts to assassinate them, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing unidentified people in the intelligence community. Russia warned in late September that defence manufacturers in European countries supplying arms to Ukraine could be considered “potential military targets”.
